articles.author: Sohail Akhter
articles.description:
Whether you're preparing for an online meeting, gaming session, or recording a podcast, ensuring your microphone works correctly is essential. Testing your microphone online is quick and easy, and you don’t need any special software. In this guide, we’ll walk you through the best ways to check if your mic is functioning properly.
Before joining a call or recording audio, it's crucial to verify:
If your microphone is detected by your device
The audio quality (clarity, volume, and background noise)
If there are any connectivity issues (for Bluetooth/USB mics)
Method 1: Using an Online Microphone Test Tool
microphone tester
Click "Allow" when the browser asks for microphone access.
Speak into your microphone—you should see real-time sound waves and hear playback.
Adjust your mic settings if the volume is too low or if there’s distortion.
Method 2: Testing via Google Meet or Zoom
Google Meet: Go to meet.google.com, click the settings (gear icon), and select "Test speaker & microphone."
Zoom: Open Zoom, go to Settings > Audio, and click "Test Mic."
Method 3: Using Windows/Mac Built-in Settings
Under Input, select your microphone and speak—you’ll see a volume indicator.
Use "Test your microphone" to check audio levels.
On Mac:
Select your mic and speak—the input level meter should respond.
No Sound? Check if the mic is properly connected and selected as the default input device.
Low Volume? Adjust mic sensitivity in your system settings or use an external amplifier.
Background Noise? Enable noise suppression in your conferencing app or use a better-quality mic.
Testing your microphone before important calls or recordings ensures smooth communication. For a quick and reliable check, try Microphone Test—it’s free, works in any browser, and provides instant feedback.
Got any other tips for mic testing? Share them in the comments below! 🎙️
articles.title: How to Test Your Microphone Online – A Simple Guide

articles.author: Eugene Oleinik
articles.description:
Voice transcription is a superpower for AI-assisted coding.
Not obvious until you try it. I picked this up from AI engineers here in Chiang Mai - they were raving about it. Now I get why.
Here's the thing about LLMs: more context = better output.
You need to dump everything related to the problem. Edge cases. Constraints. Context. The weird thing that happened yesterday that might be related.
When typing, you self-edit. You skip details that seem obvious. You write shorter prompts because typing is slow.
When speaking, you ramble. And that's the point.
Grammar doesn't matter - the AI figures it out. What matters is getting everything out of your head and into the prompt. The AI builds a complete picture from your stream of consciousness.
I rebuilt a voice transcription tool last week (Ito was shutting down, I needed an alternative). Two weekend evenings, 600 lines of Rust.
Now I use it constantly with Claude Code. Hold Fn, speak, paste. That's it.
See a problem
Hold key, describe everything about it out loud
Let Claude Code work with complete context
Your prompts will get 3x longer and your outputs will get 3x better.
FnKey (what I built): github.com/evoleinik/fnkey
articles.title: Voice Transcription is a Superpower for AI-Assisted Coding

articles.author: Sharon
articles.description:
Me



Predictive learning makes sense mathematically but how does RLHF adjust the mathematical weights in your system?
Good question - let me try to break down the actual mechanism.
So after the initial pretraining (predict the next word), RLHF works roughly like this:
Step 1: Collect comparisons
Step 2: Train a reward model
Step 3: Optimize against the reward model
The math is basically: "if changing this weight in this direction makes the reward model predict a higher score, adjust it that way - but not too much at once or you might break something."
So it's not like someone manually goes in and tweaks individual weights. It's more like: reward model says "humans would prefer this" → gradient descent math figures out which direction to adjust millions of weights → system becomes more lik…
articles.title: Claude's take on RLHF and self-doubt

articles.author: Shaidozzaman Araf
articles.description:
As a teen founder, I’ve always been fascinated by how technology can change the way we live, learn, and work. Today, I launched my first product, PippaQuiz, a small app with a big ambition: to help teachers create thoughtful, concept-driven questions in seconds and to empower students to practice real understanding instead of memorization.
The idea came from watching the struggle teachers face. Crafting questions that actually test understanding takes hours. Students often survive by memorizing rather than learning. I wanted to change that, and I wanted to start now.
How it works:
Teachers type a topic
PippaQuiz instantly generates multiple types of questions: multiple choice, short answer, reasoning-based, and creative problem-solving
Students can use it too to test themselves, creating a self-assessment loop that encourages deeper learning
What excites me most isn’t the app itself, but the bigger vision. I want to build a world where learning is more meaningful, where teachers focus on teaching and guiding, and AI handles repetitive evaluation. This is just the first step toward that future, and I see it as a startup playground where every small feature, every tweak, can have an outsized impact on real learning.
For developers and fellow builders, what matters here is the mindset: start small, build tools that solve real pain points, and don’t wait for perfect conditions to begin. I didn’t wait until college or a perfect team. I coded, iterated, and shipped. And in the process, I learned more than any textbook could teach.
I’m sharing this because I hope it inspires other young founders and builders to tackle problems they care about, no matter how ambitious they seem. Education is massive, messy, and underrated as a startup opportunity, but solving it could change millions of lives.
🔗 Try PippaQuiz
articles.title: PippaQuiz: Building the First Step Toward Smarter Education
